name: Charles Louis Fabri
title: Charles Fabri: Looking Beyond the Familiar Monuments
description: An art historian, a dancer’s encouragement, and a book that brought lesser-known Odisha monuments into a wider conversation.
author: Ahimanikya Satapathy

paragraphs.text: Charles Fabri passed a temple twice without seeing it behind the trees. In his History of the Art of Orissa, he recalls searching for the shrine at Madhaba after the poet Mayadhar Mansinha drew his attention to it. On a later visit, a local priest helped him examine its palm-leaf chronicle. The episode makes a revealing beginning to his work: a scholar following a poet’s lead, then learning from someone who cared for the temple.

Fabri’s name belongs in Odisha’s cultural history for that sustained attention, and for his encouragement of dancers seeking audiences beyond the state. His writing gave monuments and performances another public life. The people who guided him, taught the dancers and preserved the places belong in the same story.

Born in Budapest in 1899, Fabri came to Indian art through a career that crossed libraries, archaeology, museums and criticism. He worked at Leiden’s Kern Institute, joined an expedition with Aurel Stein, worked with the Archaeological Survey of India and became curator of the Lahore Museum. In Delhi, he taught art history and wrote art and theatre criticism for The Statesman. These were different ways of bringing works of art into view: finding them, organizing knowledge about them and explaining them to readers.

For Priyambada Mohanty Hejmadi, his contribution had a personal meaning. In the preface to Odissi: An Indian Classical Dance Form, written with Ahalya Hejmadi Patnaik, she remembers his encouraging response to her performance at the first Inter-University Youth Festival in 1954. She also credits him with arranging a full evening programme at Sapru House and inviting Indira Gandhi. Here criticism became practical support: helping a dancer obtain a stage and an audience.

Her account also names the training behind that performance. Banabehari Maity taught her footwork; Singhari Shyamasunder Kar taught the dance she describes as developing into modern Odissi. Mayadhar Mansingh took an active interest in compositions and translated songs into English. Fabri’s advocacy sits within this network of artistic labour. To make him the person who “discovered” Odissi would diminish the people whose work made the performance possible.

History of the Art of Orissa appeared from Orient Longman in 1974, six years after Fabri’s death. Ashok Mathur’s prefatory note records that the manuscript had been completed in 1965. Fabri’s wife, Ratna Mathur Fabri, took on the task of getting it into print after his death, but died before publication herself. Mathur credits Mayadhar Mansinha’s efforts, the sponsoring Orissa Government and the publisher with bringing it to readers. The book’s survival was a shared achievement.

Its reception was appreciative without being uncritical. Reviewing the book in July 1976, Krishna Chaitanya valued Fabri’s treatment of monuments beyond the familiar centres of Konark and Bhubaneswar. He also challenged Fabri’s proposed long Buddhist phase in Odisha’s early art, finding the evidence insufficient. He noted inconsistent dates for the illustrated Sambalpur Buddha images and questioned a rigid sequence of artistic styles. These were disputes about interpretation, not reasons to erase the documentary work.

That distinction keeps Fabri’s contribution useful. We can return to the objects he described while testing the explanations he offered. At Madhaba, the temple, the poet’s recommendation and the priest’s manuscript all mattered. Remembering those encounters gives us a fuller portrait of the scholar—and leaves the history open to the next careful reader.

corrections_and_boundaries: Do not call Fabri the discoverer or creator of Odissi; use Hejmadi’s attributed recollection and preserve teachers’ roles.
Do not date the Sapru House event1954 merely because the preceding sentence concerns1954.
Fabri died1968; book1974 is posthumous, manuscript completed1965 per original note.
Ratna Mathur Fabri, Mayadhar Mansinha, government sponsor and publisher are explicitly acknowledged; no coeditor invented.
Temple encounter is attributed to Fabri; no invented scene, dialogue, visit or present-day status.
No current dates for Buddhist art or temples are inferred from Fabri; the1976 critique remains attributed.
Mansinha is the1974 scan spelling; Mansingh follows Hejmadi’s reproduced preface.
No statement that Fabri put Odisha on the global map or was India’s first art critic.
